source.title_on_document: Designing Human and Generative AI Collaboration

supplement.where: Supporting Information is appended at PDF pp. 17–57 (its own pp. 1–41). PDF p. 17 also lists a separate MDAR Reproducibility Checklist, which is not included in this PDF.
supplement.holds: Study procedures, instructions, surveys, evaluation rubric, analysis specifications, Figure S1, and Tables S1–S12. Table S4 (PDF p. 48) supplies adjusted coefficients/SEs for originality, interestingness, writing quality, and coherence; Table S7 (PDF p. 51) supplies overall-quality coefficients/SEs; Tables S8–S9 give quality heterogeneity analyses. Main-text Figures 2 and 4 show CIs; diversity arm means and numeric CI endpoints are in main-text pp. 6–7, but the method used to calculate diversity uncertainty is not stated.

paper_design_summary: Students in an elective emerging-technologies course wrote a story without AI and then wrote another with ChatGPT under one of three randomly assigned collaboration designs: Human Confirmation, Human Creativity, or Copilot. Blinded human raters scored story quality, originality, interestingness, writing quality, and coherence; genre classification and embedding-based comparisons measured story characteristics and similarity across writers (PDF pp. 4, 6–7, 16, 18–21). An ancillary discussion compares autonomous ChatGPT DAT runs with the same cohort's baseline human DAT scores, without assigning people to AI assistance for that test (PDF p. 8).

studies.label: Classroom creative-writing experiment: three randomized AI collaboration designs

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were individually assigned to Human Confirmation, Human Creativity, or Copilot for Day 2. All wrote without AI on Day 1; the order of no-AI and AI sessions was fixed. The randomized source of variation is AI configuration, not AI availability. The classroom exercise was embedded in an elective course (PDF pp. 4, 18–20).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three AI collaboration models:
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4, Theoretical Background and Experimental Design; PDF p. 20 (SI p. 4), Figure S1.

arms.name: Human Confirmation
arms.description: Day 2: ChatGPT performs ideation, outlining, drafting, and editing. Students prompt, select, approve, or request regeneration, and may not supply their own ideas (PDF pp. 4, 18; SI B.2.1, PDF pp. 26–27).

arms.name: Human Creativity
arms.description: Day 2: students independently ideate and outline; ChatGPT drafts and edits. During production, students prompt and approve/regenerate but may not introduce additional ideas or directly write/edit (PDF pp. 4, 18–19; SI B.2.2, PDF pp. 28–29).

arms.name: Copilot
arms.description: Day 2: iterative collaboration with ChatGPT at any stage, including human ideas, writing, feedback, and editing (PDF pp. 4, 19; SI B.2.3, PDF pp. 30–31).

arms.name: Day 1 without AI (shared baseline)
arms.description: The same recruited cohort writes without AI before its AI-assisted session; this is a shared earlier measurement, not a separately randomized no-AI arm. The paper reports 278 Day 1 stories, not a separate arm-level participant count (PDF pp. 4, 21).

participants.exclusions: The reported study cohort is 285 successfully participating students, and all submitted stories were included (PDF p. 18, SI A.1). This study-level count is not an explicitly reported complete-case count for each Day 2 regression. The corpus contains 549 stories: 278 on Day 1 and 271 on Day 2 (PDF p. 21, SI A.2). Initial-survey characteristics have N = 280 (PDF p. 11, Table 1). Reasons for missing stories/surveys, numbers completing both days, per-arm counts, and regression-specific participant counts are not stated; no attrition totals have been derived. Stories exceeding the recommended time were retained, including 7 participants on Day 1 and 3 on Day 2 (PDF p. 18).
participants.who: Students in an elective course on emerging technologies, participating in a classroom exercise for course credits; the university hosting the course is not explicitly named. Nine additional student research assistants served as external raters and are not added to the writer count (PDF pp. 18–19, SI A.1).
participants.quote: A total of 285 students successfully participated in the experiment.
participants.locator: PDF p. 18 (SI p. 2), A.1 Participants and inclusion of all submitted stories; PDF p. 21 (SI p. 5), A.2 corpus counts; PDF p. 11, Table 1.

ai_tool.how_used: Students directly prompted ChatGPT under their assigned collaboration rules after prompt-engineering training. Copilot allowed open collaboration; Human Confirmation restricted users to prompting/judgment; Human Creativity reserved ideation/outlining for humans and delegated drafting/editing to ChatGPT. AI remained available during production of all scored Day 2 stories. GPT-4o was separately used to classify story genres, and text-embedding-3-large to measure story similarity (PDF pp. 4, 6, 16, 18–19).

task.description: Write a new 1,000-word short story of any genre in each session, with a seven-sequence narrative guide; Day 1 unassisted and Day 2 under the assigned AI collaboration design (PDF pp. 4, 18–20).
task.duration: Two-day study. Main text and recruitment description specify 105-minute writing sessions; Figure S1 also specifies 105 minutes. SI A.1's Day 1 and Day 2 task paragraphs instead say 75 minutes. Recruitment also specifies 15-minute surveys (PDF pp. 4, 18–20).

outcomes.name: Overall story quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The overall assessment asks whether the story conveys its ideas creatively, interestingly, coherently, and with good writing (PDF p. 41, SI B.4 Q7). Coded as overall_creativity because this is the paper's holistic assessment of creative output, although its label is Overall Quality. Adjusted and unadjusted specifications in Table S7 are variants of this outcome. Figure 2B/D/E and Tables S8–S9 examine heterogeneity by baseline quality/DAT; Table S8 uses participant-level story-average ratings and is not a separate outcome. Two fellow participants and two external student research assistants independently rated each story, blind to writer identity and AI condition, on a 1–7 scale (PDF pp. 4, 19, 41). The main arm-comparison regressions use individual evaluations, not participant averages; covariates are DAT score, writing experience, writing ability, and English proficiency (PDF p. 23, SI A.3). No clustering by writer/story/rater or mixed model is stated. n_units = 2,196 is the entire two-day rating corpus, not a stated Day 2 regression sample size (PDF pp. 11, 21).

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity of stories within each condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity between a story embedding and the average embedding of all other stories in the same condition. The model is OpenAI text-embedding-3-large. Day 1's unassisted corpus is compared with each of the three Day 2 condition corpora (PDF p. 16, Figure 4C caption). The paper says all stories were classified/analyzed. n_units = 549 denotes the complete two-day story corpus (278 without AI and 271 with AI), not a per-contrast or per-arm sample size; arm-specific counts are not printed (PDF pp. 6, 21). Each similarity score belongs to one story, rather than one pair of stories.

contrasts.reported: Human Creativity: mean = 0.710, 95% CI [0.700, 0.720]; Human Confirmation: mean = 0.779, 95% CI [0.767, 0.790]. These are raw similarity means and arm-specific intervals, not a CI for the difference. Main text describes the differences as statistically significant without reporting exact tests. Direction is coded for diversity, the reverse of similarity.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity to the leave-one-out condition centroid; reported as condition means and 95% CIs.
diversity_detail.computed_over: For each story, its embedding versus the mean embedding of all other stories in the same condition; separate pools for Day 1 without AI and the Day 2 Human Confirmation, Human Creativity, and Copilot conditions (PDF p. 16, Figure 4C caption).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are printed and differences are described as statistically significant, but no test statistic, exact p value, resampling procedure, or CI construction method is supplied (PDF pp. 6–7, 15–16).
diversity_detail.notes: Higher raw similarity means less across-person diversity. Contrast directions below are reversed to express diversity benefits; raw reported means are unchanged. Each story shares comparison stories with other scores, and no adjustment for that dependence is stated.

outcomes.name: Genre similarity of stories within each condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4o classifies each story into one or more of nine fiction genres. Genres form a binary vector; the analysis computes its cosine similarity to the average genre vector of all other stories in the same condition (PDF pp. 6, 16). category_count is the closest form vocabulary for similarity calculated from coded genre indicators; it is not a text embedding measure. The paper says all stories were classified/analyzed. n_units = 549 denotes the complete two-day story corpus (278 without AI and 271 with AI), not a per-contrast or per-arm sample size; arm-specific counts are not printed (PDF pp. 6, 21). Each similarity score belongs to one story, rather than one pair of stories.

contrasts.reported: Human Creativity: mean = 0.533, 95% CI [0.526, 0.539]; Human Confirmation: mean = 0.592, 95% CI [0.585, 0.598]. These are arm-specific intervals for raw similarity. No direct pairwise coefficient, difference SE, or exact p value is printed. Direction is coded for diversity.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of a nine-dimensional binary genre vector to the leave-one-out condition mean genre vector.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Not applicable: GPT-4o supplies genre classifications; similarities use binary genre vectors, not language-model embeddings.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each story's genre vector versus the average genre vector of all other stories in its condition; separate Day 1 baseline and Day 2 AI-design pools (PDF p. 16, Figure 4B caption).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Condition means with 95% CIs; the text describes Human Confirmation versus unassisted writing as significant and the other AI conditions versus unassisted writing as nonsignificant. The CI/test construction and dependence adjustment are not specified (PDF pp. 6, 15–16).
diversity_detail.notes: Directions express diversity, so higher similarity is coded as lower diversity. Direct AI-design contrasts have no printed difference SE or exact p value.

diversity_detail.metric: Condition-level percentages in nine genre categories, with percentage-point differences from unassisted writing; no single scalar diversity index.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Genre indicators aggregated across all stories within each of the three Day 2 AI designs and across all Day 1 unassisted stories (PDF pp. 15–16, Figure 4A).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Figure 4A prints percentages and percentage-point changes but no confidence intervals, SEs, or tests. Text describes genre shifts without supplying their test results (PDF p. 6).
diversity_detail.notes: A change in genre mix does not itself establish an increase or decrease in overall diversity, so directions are mixed. Rounded percentages and changes are copied separately exactly as printed, including -0; differences have not been recalculated.

studies.label: Ancillary autonomous ChatGPT versus human baseline DAT benchmark (same human sample)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No people were assigned to AI assistance for the DAT comparison. The authors separately administered DAT to ChatGPT and compared its scores descriptively with the S1 participants' baseline scores (PDF p. 8).
assignment.quote: We also administered the DAT test to ChatGPT 3.5—the version of the tool that was used by participants.

arms.name: ChatGPT 3.5 autonomous DAT
arms.description: Model independently completes DAT; twenty tests are reported. These are model runs, not participants (PDF p. 8).

arms.name: S1 human baseline DAT
arms.description: Writing-study participants take the DAT on Day 1 before AI-assisted writing, then report their first score in the initial survey (PDF pp. 19, 35). Table 1 reports N = 280 for DAT score.

participants.exclusions: N = 280 is the DAT initial-survey sample printed in Table 1. The paper reports a larger overall writing-study cohort, but does not explain missing DAT scores. Twenty ChatGPT tests are model observations and are not included in the people count (PDF pp. 8, 11).
participants.who: The same elective-course students as S1, restricted to the initial-survey DAT score sample; no new human recruitment (PDF pp. 8, 11, 18–19, 35).
participants.locator: PDF p. 11, Table 1, Personal Characteristics / DAT Score row; PDF p. 8, Discussion.

ai_tool.how_used: Autonomous completion of the DAT for a descriptive benchmark; no human receives AI help during this benchmark. The model's prompting, sampling settings, and procedure for independent runs are not given (PDF p. 8).

task.description: Divergent Association Task: produce ten largely unrelated words/nouns, with verbal creativity measured by semantic distance. Human participants took the test online and reported their first score (PDF pp. 19, 35).
task.duration: The human DAT typically takes 2 to 4 minutes; model timing is not stated (PDF p. 35, SI B.3.2).

outcomes.name: Divergent Association Task score
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: DAT measures verbal creativity through semantic distance between the supplied words (PDF p. 19). Human participants reported their first website-generated score rather than a subjective creativity rating (PDF p. 35). The comparison is autonomous model output versus unassisted human output, not an effect of assistance. Table 1's human mean/SD are kept distinct from the rounded mean given in the discussion. No total mixed human/model observation count is derived.

contrasts.reported: Discussion: ChatGPT average DAT = 85.7, range 82 to 88, across twenty tests; human DAT mean = 82.2, range 65 to 95. Table 1 separately prints human DAT N = 280, Mean = 82.28, SD = 7.13. No model SD, comparison SE, CI, test statistic, or p value is reported; higher describes the means only.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8, Discussion, second finding; PDF p. 11, Table 1, DAT Score row.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No overlap with another paper is stated. Within this paper, S2 reuses the initial-survey DAT scores of the S1 writing-study cohort; these are not newly recruited participants.
sample_overlap.quote: participants in our study had DAT scores between 65 and 95, with a mean of 82.2.
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 8, Discussion; PDF p. 11, Table 1; PDF p. 35 (SI p. 19), B.3.2.

company_involvement.description: No company funding, author affiliation, or other company involvement is disclosed. Authors declare no competing interests; funding is stated as not applicable. Use of OpenAI products is the intervention/measurement technology, not a disclosed company role.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1, author affiliations and Competing Interest Statement; PDF p. 9, Acknowledgments/Funding.

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigns students to three generative-AI configurations (PDF p. 4; Figure S1, PDF p. 20); the course-embedded exercise is coded field_rct (PDF p. 18, SI A.1). The paper reports 285 successfully participating students and inclusion of all submitted stories (PDF p. 18), with 549 stories across days, including 271 on Day 2 (PDF p. 21); the study clearly exceeds 50 people, although per-arm and regression-specific participant counts are not stated. Human ratings and computed similarity measures score the produced stories (PDF pp. 4, 16, 19, 41). Core eligibility applies to randomized ai_design contrasts. Day 2 versus Day 1 contrasts are fixed-order before/after evidence, not randomized ai_vs_bau; there is no after_ai outcome. S2 is an ancillary ai_vs_human benchmark and does not establish core eligibility.

one_line_finding: Human Creativity and Copilot exceeded Human Confirmation in adjusted overall story quality by 0.3376 (SE 0.106) and 0.3158 (SE 0.105), respectively (PDF p. 51, Table S7), while their story-similarity means were 0.710 and 0.743 versus 0.779 for Human Confirmation (PDF p. 7).
open_questions: What are the per-arm randomized and analyzed participant counts, the Day 2 regression complete-case counts, and the reasons for missing stories/survey data? The reported 285 is the overall participating cohort, not a separately printed regression sample size (PDF pp. 18, 21; Table 1, p. 11).
Were the rating-level standard errors clustered by participant/story or rater? SI A.3 and Tables S4/S7 do not state such adjustment (PDF pp. 23, 48, 51).

How were the genre- and semantic-similarity confidence intervals and significance statements calculated, and did they account for dependence induced by the common condition centroids (PDF pp. 6–7, 15–16)?
Which writing time is correct: 105 minutes in the main text, recruitment description, and Figure S1, or 75 minutes in the SI task paragraphs (PDF pp. 4, 18–20)?
What is the date/version of the saved manuscript? No version identifier is printed on its cover pages (PDF pp. 1, 17).
notes: Screened 2026-10-09. Locators use 1-based pages of the complete PDF; SI printed page numbers are additionally supplied. The full markdown, including all supplementary methods, instructions, tables, and references, was read; conversion-duplicated table cells were grouped for readability. Cited design/count pages and all reported numerical sources were checked against PDF text/tables; rasterized Figures 2, 4, and S1 were also inspected in memory. No effects, SEs, sample sizes, or CI endpoints were derived. The 285 count is retained as the paper's overall successful participant cohort, while arm-level and contrast-specific people counts remain null. Counts of stories and evaluations are recorded as units and qualified by their two-day scope. There is one recruited human writing experiment; S2 separately records the ancillary model-versus-human DAT dataset and shares the human baseline sample. Nonrandomized day comparisons are distinguished with comparison_type before_after. Main Day 2 contrasts retain the paper's Human Confirmation reference group and printed latter-minus-former orientation; the paper does not name one AI configuration as the default. Overall quality and semantic similarity are treated as the main outcomes for the atlas's two relevant questions; no preregistration or formal primary/secondary hierarchy is stated. Self-reported completion times, process/AI satisfaction, perceived AI contribution, and qualitative feedback are outside the scored-output outcome list. Baseline characteristics and subgroup/robustness versions of quality are not additional outcomes. Data/code URL is printed on PDF p. 9 and was recorded without fetching it. Genre-count richness is coded other because it counts genres within one story; genre-distribution percentages are recorded as a categorical across_people descriptor, with no scalar diversity direction. The ancillary S2 DAT comparison is descriptive and contributes no assistance estimate; its human scores are not independent of S1.
